Hey! You can’t just add the tops *and* the bottoms because fractions aren’t “pairs” that behave like whole numbers.  

Think of \(\frac{3}{x}\) as “3 lots of size \(1/x\)” and \(\frac{2}{x+1}\) as “2 lots of size \(1/(x+1)\)”. The two “lot‑sizes” are different, so you must first make them the same size before you can combine the lots.  

The way to do that is to find a common denominator (the LCD). Here the LCD is \(x(x+1)\). Rewrite each fraction with that denominator, then add the numerators:

\[
\frac{3}{x}=\frac{3(x+1)}{x(x+1)},\qquad
\frac{2}{x+1}=\frac{2x}{x(x+1)}.
\]

Now the denominators match, so you can add the numerators: \(\frac{3(x+1)+2x}{x(x+1)}\).  

If you ever tried the “add tops and bottoms” trick with numbers, e.g. \(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3} = \frac{1+1}{2+3} = \frac{2}{5}\), you can check that \(\frac{2}{5}=0.4\) while the true sum is \(\frac{5}{6}\approx0.833\). The difference shows why the shortcut fails.  

Keep using the LCD method—you’re already strong at distributing, so the algebra will be smooth once the fractions line up!
